claim: Mutational antigenic profiling quantifies how every amino-acid mutation to HA affects viral neutralization.
source: As illustrated in Figure 1, this approach quantifies how every amino-acid mutation to HA affects viral neutralization.
evidence: The manuscript describes the method and Figure 1 illustrates the approach, providing both textual and visual support.

claim: The Perth/2009 virus was the H3N2 component of the influenza vaccine from 2010 to 2012.
source: Here, we perform mutational antigenic profiling using mutant virus libraries with the HA from A/Perth/16/2009 (Lee et al., 2018), which was the H3N2 component of the influenza vaccine from 2010 to 2012 (WHO, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2019.

claim: Four monoclonal antibodies (5A01, 4C01, 4F03, and 1C04) were isolated from humans who had received the 2010–2011 trivalent influenza vaccine.
source: To validate mutational antigenic profiling for these viral libraries, we first performed selections with four monoclonal antibodies isolated from humans who had received the 2010–2011 trivalent influenza vaccine (Zost et al., 2017; Henry Dunand et al., 2015). These four antibodies were 037-10036-5A01, 034-10040-4C01, 028-10134-4F03, and 041-10047-1C04, hereafter referred to as '5A01', '4C01', '4F03', and '1C04', respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zost et al., 2017 and Henry Dunand et al., 2015.

claim: Two of the four monoclonal antibodies target near the receptor-binding pocket, while two target lower on HA's head.
source: Based on binding assays to a small HA mutant panel, two antibodies target near the receptor-binding pocket, while two antibodies target lower on HA's head (Zost et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zost et al., 2019.

claim: The selected mutations were consistent across biological replicates with independently generated mutant virus libraries.
source: Importantly, the selected mutations were consistent across the biological replicates with independently generated mutant virus libraries (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), confirming that our approach systematically maps the antigenic effects of all mutations rather than simply selecting one-off viral mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The strongly selected mutations occurred mostly at sites classically categorized as antigenic region B.
source: The strongly selected mutations occurred mostly at sites that are classically categorized as antigenic region B (Supplementary file 1; Wiley et al., 1981; Wu and Wilson, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wiley et al., 1981 and Wu and Wilson, 2017, and reference to Supplementary file 1.

claim: Although the antibodies all targeted the same antigenic region of HA, they selected different escape mutations.
source: However, although the antibodies all targeted the same antigenic region of HA, they selected different escape mutations (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: K160T reduces neutralization by antibody 5A01 but has no effect on neutralization by antibody 4C01.
source: For instance, K160T reduces neutralization by antibody 5A01 but has no effect on neutralization by antibody 4C01 despite the fact that both antibodies target a similar region of HA (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Four sera were identified that completely neutralized virus with the wild-type Perth/2009 HA at a dilution of ≥1:40.
source: We therefore screened the neutralizing activity of sera collected from 16 healthy adults between 2008 and 2010, and identified four sera that completely neutralized virus with the wild-type Perth/2009 HA at a dilution of ≥1:40 (which is the HAI titer traditionally assumed to reduce risk of infection; Hobson et al., 1972).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hobson et al., 1972.

claim: The pre-screened sera had inhibitory concentrations 50% (IC50s) ranging from ~1:800 to ~1:3000.
source: Notably, this pre-screening means that all the sera that we characterized had high neutralizing activity, with inhibitory concentrations 50% (IC50s) ranging from ~1:800 to ~1:3000 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Despite being polyclonal, each serum strongly selected single escape mutations.
source: Despite being polyclonal, each serum strongly selected single escape mutations (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The selected mutations occurred at a relatively small number of sites, predominantly in the portion of HA classically categorized as antigenic region B.
source: The selected mutations occurred at a relatively small number of sites, predominantly in the portion of HA classically categorized as antigenic region B (Figure 3A,C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A,C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: For three individuals (the 21-year-old, 64-year-old, and 65-year-old), the strongest escape mutation had a >10-fold effect on neutralization.
source: For three individuals (the 21-year-old, 64-year-old, and 65-year-old), the strongest escape mutation had a >10-fold effect on neutralization, and for the remaining individual (the 53-year-old) the strongest escape mutation had a ∼5-fold effect (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The antigenic effect of the strongest escape mutant from three of the polyclonal sera was comparable to that of strongest escape mutant from the monoclonal antibody 5A01.
source: Amazingly, the antigenic effect of the strongest escape mutant from three of the polyclonal sera was comparable to that of strongest escape mutant from the monoclonal antibody 5A01 (compare Figure 2B to Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of data in Figure 2B and Figure 3B.

claim: The exact mutations that mediated escape differed markedly across sera.
source: However, the exact mutations that mediated escape differed markedly across sera (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: F193D escaped viral neutralization by the serum from the 21-year-old individual by >10-fold but had no effect for the serum from the 64-year-old.
source: For instance, F193D escaped viral neutralization by the serum from the 21-year-old individual by >10-fold—but had no effect for the serum from the 64-year-old (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: F159G escaped neutralization by the 64-year-old's serum but had minimal effect on neutralization by the 53-year-old.
source: Similarly, F159G escaped neutralization by the 64-year-old's serum but had minimal effect on neutralization by the 53-year-old (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: K160T moderately enhanced neutralization resistance to all four sera.
source: In fact, the only viral mutation that had a consistent antigenic effect across individuals is K160T, which moderately enhanced neutralization resistance to all four sera.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The maps of immune selection were highly similar for the two serum samples from the 53-year-old individual collected two months apart.
source: Figure 4 shows that the maps of immune selection were highly similar for the two samples, consistent with the expectation that the specificity of the serum was stable over the 2 months.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The serum from the 25-year-old individual strongly selected escape mutants in the Perth/2009 library even pre-vaccination.
source: The serum from one individual (the 25-year-old) strongly selected escape mutants in the Perth/2009 library even pre-vaccination (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The 25-year-old individual's serum had the most potent pre-vaccination neutralizing activity against Perth/2009, with an IC50 of ∼1:800.
source: This individual's serum also had the most potent pre-vaccination neutralizing activity against Perth/2009, with an IC50 of ∼1:800 (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: F159G reduced neutralization by the 25-year-old's pre-vaccination serum by over an order of magnitude.
source: The mutation most strongly selected by the pre-vaccination serum (F159G) reduced neutralization by over an order of magnitude (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Vaccination of the 25-year-old individual substantially enhanced the serum's potency, dropping the IC50 to ∼1:10,000.
source: Vaccination of this individual substantially enhanced the serum's potency, dropping the IC50 to ∼1:10,000—but F159G continued to have the largest effect on neutralization, still reducing the IC50 by over an order of magnitude (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: The maps of immune selection were very similar for all post-infection ferret sera.
source: In stark contrast to the person-to-person variation of the human sera, the maps of immune selection were very similar for all post-infection ferret sera (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The differences between ferrets infected with Perth/2009 and Victoria/2011 viruses are smaller than the differences among nearly all the human sera.
source: This was true even for the ferret infected with Victoria/2011 rather than Perth/2009 virus: visual comparison of Figure 6A and Figure 3A suggests that the differences between ferrets infected with these two antigenically distinct H3N2 viruses are smaller than the differences among nearly all the human sera.
evidence: The claim is supported by visual comparison of data in Figure 6A and Figure 3A.

claim: The ferret sera had a beta diversity of 1.12, while human sera from 2009–2010 had a beta diversity of 1.38 and post-vaccination sera from 2015 had a beta diversity of 1.60.
source: This analysis confirmed that the ferret sera (beta diversity of 1.12) were more consistent in the sites where they exerted selection than the human sera from either 2009–2010 or post-vaccination from 2015 (beta diversity of 1.38 and 1.60, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by beta diversity calculations performed on the data.

claim: The strongest selection from the ferret sera focused on sites 189 and 193, with mutations K189D and F193D tending to have a ∼5 to 10-fold effect on neutralization.
source: The strongest selection from the ferret sera focused on sites 189 and 193, with mutations K189D and F193D tending to have a ∼5 to 10-fold effect on neutralization (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Sites 189 and 193 are important for antigenic recognition by ferret sera.
source: Prior work has also noted that these two sites are important for antigenic recognition by ferret sera (Koel et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Koel et al., 2013.

claim: The site where mutations were most strongly selected by all the ferret sera (site 189) had an appreciable antigenic effect for only one of the human sera.
source: The site where mutations were most strongly selected by all the ferret sera (site 189) had an appreciable antigenic effect for only one of the human sera.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of data across figures.

claim: Site 193 had an antigenic effect for less than half the human sera.
source: The other site where mutations were consistently and strongly selected by the ferret sera (site 193) had an antigenic effect for less than half the human sera.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of data across figures.

claim: Many sites of mutations strongly selected by human sera (such as 157, 159, and 160) had little antigenic effect for the ferret sera.
source: The converse was also true: many sites of mutations strongly selected by human sera (such as 157, 159, and 160) had little antigenic effect for the ferret sera.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of data across figures.

claim: Even when the serum was spiked with the lowest concentration of antibody, the mutational antigenic profiling showed signals of selection at sites targeted by the antibody.
source: Even when the serum was spiked with the lowest concentration of antibody, the mutational antigenic profiling showed signals of selection at sites targeted by the antibody (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: At the middle antibody concentration, selection from the antibody exceeded that from the serum, although both were still apparent.
source: At the middle antibody concentration, selection from the antibody exceeded that from the serum, although both were still apparent (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: At the highest antibody concentration, selection at antibody-targeted sites completely overwhelmed selection at serum-targeted sites.
source: At the highest antibody concentration, selection at antibody-targeted sites completely overwhelmed selection at serum-targeted sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The strongest serum-escape mutations (F159G and F193D) actually sensitize the virus to neutralization by the antibody.
source: Part of the reason the antibody so readily dominates the selection in Figure 7A may be that the strongest serum-escape mutations (F159G and F193D) actually sensitize the virus to neutralization by the antibody (Figure 7B), a result reminiscent of earlier work showing synergistic effects of mixing antibodies (Lubeck and Gerhard, 1982; Webster and Laver, 1980).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B and citations to Lubeck and Gerhard, 1982 and Webster and Laver, 1980.

claim: There has been substantial amino-acid evolution at nine of the sites strongly selected by the human sera.
source: There has been substantial amino-acid evolution (new variants reaching ≥ 5% frequency) at nine of the sites strongly selected by the human sera (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claim: During the evolution of human H3N2 influenza virus, new amino-acid variants have reached >10% frequency at all five sites (144, 157, 159, 189, and 193) where the single largest-effect mutations occurred.
source: Across all sera that strongly selected mutations, the single largest-effect mutations occurred at five sites: 144, 157, 159, 189, and 193 (Figure 3A and Figure 5A). During the evolution of human H3N2 influenza virus, new amino-acid variants have reached >10% frequency at all these sites (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A, Figure 5A, and Figure 8.

claim: K160T introduces a N-linked glycosylation motif near the top of HA's head.
source: The one HA mutation with an antigenic effect across almost all human sera we examined was K160T, which consistently caused a moderate increase in neutralization resistance (Figure 3A,B). This mutation introduces a N-linked glycosylation motif near the top of HA's head.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A,B and knowledge of glycosylation motifs.

claim: K160T appeared among natural human H3N2 viruses in late 2013 and is now present in the majority of circulating viruses.
source: K160T appeared among natural human H3N2 viruses in late 2013 and is now present in the majority of circulating viruses (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claim: K160T and mutations at three of the sites strongly selected by just some sera (144, 159, and 193) distinguish the 3C2.A and 3C3.A clades that currently circulate in humans.
source: In addition, K160T and mutations at three of the sites strongly selected by just some sera (144, 159, and 193) distinguish the 3C2.A and 3C3.A clades that currently circulate in humans (Bedford and Neher, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bedford and Neher, 2018.

claim: Many sera are highly focused, and select single viral mutations that reduce neutralization by over an order of magnitude.
source: We have mapped the selection that polyclonal human sera exert on all amino-acid mutations to a H3N2 influenza virus HA. Many sera are highly focused, and select single viral mutations that reduce neutralization by over an order of magnitude.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The targets of serum selection vary widely from person to person.
source: A striking result is that the targets of serum selection vary widely from person to person.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Viral mutations that greatly reduce neutralization by one individual's serum sometimes have no effect for another individual's serum.
source: Viral mutations that greatly reduce neutralization by one individual's serum sometimes have no effect for another individual's serum, which is instead affected by different mutations.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The sera profiled predominantly focus on the portion of HA classically categorized as antigenic region B.
source: The sera that we profiled predominantly focus on the portion of HA classically categorized as antigenic region B, consistent with other studies reporting that this region is immunodominant in recent H3N2 strains (Popova et al., 2012; Chambers et al., 2015; Broecker et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and citations to Popova et al., 2012; Chambers et al., 2015; Broecker et al., 2018.

claim: Different mutations in the same antigenic region can have very different effects across sera.
source: But our results show that different mutations in the same antigenic region can have very different effects across sera.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The specificity of human sera is more fine-grained than the classical categorization of HA into antigenic regions.
source: The specificity of human sera is therefore more fine-grained than the classical categorization of HA into antigenic regions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing variation in mutation effects within antigenic regions.

claim: Neutralizing serum activity is a strong correlate of protection against influenza.
source: But despite these caveats, many studies have shown that neutralizing serum activity is a strong correlate of protection against influenza (Hobson et al., 1972; Wagner et al., 1987; Krammer, 2019), so mapping selection from such serum provides an important if incomplete picture of the selection that human immunity imposes on the virus.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hobson et al., 1972; Wagner et al., 1987; Krammer, 2019.

claim: Multiple studies have shown that relatively few clonotypes comprise the majority of the anti-HA serum repertoire of a single individual.
source: Indeed, multiple studies have shown that relatively few clonotypes comprise the majority of the anti-HA serum repertoire of a single individual (Andrews et al., 2015a; Lee et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Andrews et al., 2015a; Lee et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2019.

claim: As an individual ages, much of the antibody response is diverted to non-neutralizing epitopes because sites targeted by potently neutralizing antibodies change during viral evolution, while non-neutralizing epitopes are more often conserved.
source: In support of the second idea, recent work has shown that as an individual ages, much of the antibody response is diverted to non-neutralizing epitopes because sites targeted by potently neutralizing antibodies change during viral evolution, while non-neutralizing epitopes are more often conserved (Henry et al., 2019; Ranjeva et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Henry et al., 2019; Ranjeva et al., 2019.

claim: Exposure history shapes human immunity to influenza.
source: Prior work has shown that exposure history shapes human immunity to influenza (Li et al., 2013; Andrews et al., 2015b; Gostic et al., 2016; Cobey and Hensley, 2017), and variation in exposure history is a plausible cause of the person-to-person variation we observe in the antigenic effects of viral mutations.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2013; Andrews et al., 2015b; Gostic et al., 2016; Cobey and Hensley, 2017.

claim: The lack of variation in immune selection among ferrets that have been experimentally infected just once with a defined viral strain suggests a role for exposure history in person-to-person variation.
source: A role for exposure history is further suggested by the lack of variation in immune selection among ferrets that have been experimentally infected just once with a defined viral strain.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of human and ferret data.

claim: The differences between human and ferret sera underscore the shortcomings of using singly infected ferrets as the primary tool for characterizing viral antigenicity.
source: In either case, the differences between human and ferret sera underscore the shortcomings of using singly infected ferrets as the primary tool for characterizing viral antigenicity, as has previously been shown for H1N1 (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and a citation to Li et al., 2013.

claim: Infection of humans with influenza virus elicits potent neutralizing antibodies targeting the viral hemagglutinin (HA) protein.
source: Infection of humans with influenza virus elicits potent neutralizing antibodies targeting the viral hemagglutinin (HA) protein.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about influenza immunity.

claim: These antibodies provide long-lasting immunity against the viral strain that elicited them.
source: These antibodies provide long-lasting immunity against the viral strain that elicited them (Couch, 1975; Davies et al., 1982; Couch and Kasel, 1983; Yu et al., 2008; Krammer, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Couch, 1975; Davies et al., 1982; Couch and Kasel, 1983; Yu et al., 2008; Krammer, 2019.

claim: The effectiveness of immunity against future strains is rapidly degraded by viral antigenic evolution.
source: Unfortunately, the effectiveness of this immunity against future strains is rapidly degraded by viral antigenic evolution (Bedford et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2004), such that the typical human is infected by influenza virus roughly every 5 years (Couch and Kasel, 1983; Kucharski et al., 2015; Ranjeva et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bedford et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2004; Couch and Kasel, 1983; Kucharski et al., 2015; Ranjeva et al., 2019.

claim: The typical human is infected by influenza virus roughly every 5 years.
source: Unfortunately, the effectiveness of this immunity against future strains is rapidly degraded by viral antigenic evolution (Bedford et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2004), such that the typical human is infected by influenza virus roughly every 5 years (Couch and Kasel, 1983; Kucharski et al., 2015; Ranjeva et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Couch and Kasel, 1983; Kucharski et al., 2015; Ranjeva et al., 2019.

claim: It is easy to experimentally select mutant viruses that escape neutralization by individual monoclonal antibodies.
source: Classic studies of this evolutionary process demonstrated that it is easy to experimentally select mutant viruses that escape neutralization by individual monoclonal antibodies (Yewdell et al., 1979; Laver et al., 1979; Webster and Laver, 1980; Gerhard et al., 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yewdell et al., 1979; Laver et al., 1979; Webster and Laver, 1980; Gerhard et al., 1981.

claim: Monoclonal antibodies target a variety of non-overlapping regions on HA, such that no single viral mutation can escape a mix of antibodies targeting distinct regions.
source: But these same studies also found that monoclonal antibodies target a variety of non-overlapping regions on HA, such that no single viral mutation can escape a mix of antibodies targeting distinct regions (Yewdell et al., 1979; Laver et al., 1979; Webster and Laver, 1980; Caton et al., 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yewdell et al., 1979; Laver et al., 1979; Webster and Laver, 1980; Caton et al., 1982.

claim: One explanation proposes that polyclonal immunity simply selects mutations that provide generalized neutralization resistance by increasing receptor avidity, without necessarily abrogating antibody binding.
source: One explanation proposes that polyclonal immunity simply selects mutations that provide generalized neutralization resistance by increasing receptor avidity, without necessarily abrogating antibody binding (Yewdell et al., 1986; Hensley et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yewdell et al., 1986; Hensley et al., 2009.

claim: Another explanation proposes that human immunity is sufficiently focused on one epitope in HA that single viral mutations can appreciably reduce binding by the mix of antibodies in polyclonal sera.
source: Another explanation proposes that human immunity is sufficiently focused on one epitope in HA that single viral mutations can appreciably reduce binding by the mix of antibodies in polyclonal sera. This latter explanation has been shown to be true for the immunity of certain individuals against H1N1 influenza virus (Li et al., 2013; Linderman et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2015; Davis et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2013; Linderman et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2015; Davis et al., 2018.

claim: Mass spectrometry studies show that HA-binding antibodies after vaccination are often dominated by relatively few 'clonotypes'.
source: It is also supported by mass spectrometry studies showing that HA-binding antibodies after vaccination are often dominated by relatively few 'clonotypes' (Lee et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2019), and studies with ferret sera suggesting that mutations to a small number of HA residues near the receptor binding pocket can lead to large antigenic changes (Koel et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2019.

claim: Studies with ferret sera suggest that mutations to a small number of HA residues near the receptor binding pocket can lead to large antigenic changes.
source: It is also supported by mass spectrometry studies showing that HA-binding antibodies after vaccination are often dominated by relatively few 'clonotypes' (Lee et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2019), and studies with ferret sera suggesting that mutations to a small number of HA residues near the receptor binding pocket can lead to large antigenic changes (Koel et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Koel et al., 2013.

claim: The 'wild-type' Perth/2009 HA used in this study has two amino-acid mutations (G78D and T212I) relative to the most common Perth/2009 HA sequences in Genbank.
source: The 'wild-type' Perth/2009 HA used in this study is that from Lee et al. (2018). This HA has two amino-acid mutations (G78D and T212I) relative to the most common Perth/2009 HA sequences in Genbank (there are several variants in Genbank).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2018.

claim: These two mutations (G78D and T212I) improve viral growth in cell culture.
source: These two mutations improve viral growth in cell culture (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2018.

claim: All other genes in this virus were derived from A/WSN/1933, a H1N1 strain that grows efficiently in cell culture.
source: As described below, all other genes in this virus were derived from A/WSN/1933, a H1N1 strain that grows efficiently in cell culture and was heavily adapted from its original human isolate predecessor by passaging in mouse brain in the lab (Stuart-Harris, 1939; Sun et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stuart-Harris, 1939; Sun et al., 2010.
